newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 25.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- KRUPP DROPS BID FOR THYSSEN

Krupp Hoesch, the German steel and engineering group, unexpectedly dropped its hostile bid for Thyssen Monday and said that it would instead enter into talks to form a joint venture with its larger rival in the steel sector. A joint statement from the two groups, which are both active in the automotive parts and distribution sectors, said they would look at extending their co-operation to other areas. The announcement last week of Krupp's DM13.6 billion bid for Thyssen provoked an angry reaction from employees and politicians and caused concern that hostile bids might become widespread in Germany.
-- UK ACHIEVES BIGGEST SURPLUS FOR 10 YEARS

The announcement Monday of the biggest balance of payments surplus for 10 years increased the focus of the general election campaign on the sustainability of the UK's economic recovery. The UK's current account was 873 million stg in the black in the last quarter of 1996, according to data from the Office for National Statistics. The deficit for 1996 as a whole stood at 14 million stg, the strongest performance since 1985. Chancellor Kenneth Clarke said, "This time we have healthy growth which is not running into the balance of payments problems which caused past booms to turn into bust." However, Labour pointed to figures indicating a decline in investment in manufacturing and warned that the economic recovery could be short-lived.
-- PRUDENTIAL WINS AUCTION FOR SCOTTISH AMICABLE

Prudential Corporation is today expected to be announced as the winner of the 2 billion stg auction for mutual life insurer Scottish Amicable. Prudential's bid is thought to have been selected against competition from Abbey National and Australian Mutual Provident. Details of the bid, which will offer bonuses to Scottish Amicable's 1.1 million policy holders, will be revealed Tuesday. The acquisition, which is in line with Prudential's aim of strengthening its life business, will bolster its distribution through independent financial advisors and extend its product range.
-- PEP SELLING 'BONANZA' FAILS TO MATERIALISE

Sales of Personal Equity Plans are running well below last year's levels because of investors' fears of a fall in share prices. Figures from the Autif trade body show that private investors spending on unit trust Peps fell 17% in February against the same period last year in spite of heavy advertising spending by the industry. "We thought it was going to be a bonanza Pep selling season, because of the proximity of the general election, but we underestimated the effect of high share prices," said Bridget Cleverly, assistant director at Schroders, the UK's largest unit trust manager.
-- CALL FOR EARLY PFI LEGISLATION AFTER ELECTION

Lawyers representing private finance initiative consortia have told government and opposition politicians that a change in the law is required early in the next parliament to ensure the success of the initiative in local government. Representatives of banks and companies involved in PFI projects have drawn up a draft form of words designed to remove any doubts of the legality of local authorities' right to enter into such contracts. The move follows a High Court ruling last year that two councils could not be forced to repay loans which they had exceeded their powers in guaranteeing.
-- MANX 'WHISKEY' DISTILLERS SUFFER UNCLOUDED JUDGEMENT

A High Court judge ruled Monday that Glen Kella, a clear alcoholic spirit distilled on the Isle of Man, cannot be marketed as "Manx whiskey". Glen Kella's production process falls outside EU regulations governing which spirits qualify as whiskey, or whisky if distilled in Scotland, the judge said. He added that to approve the marketing of Glen Kella as whiskey would risk the "erosion of the integrity of the reputation or 'aura' of true whisky". The case was brought by the Scotch Whisky Association and market leaders Allied Domecq and United Distillers.
-- TRAIN OPERATOR REHIRES DRIVERS

Regional Railways North East, the privatised train operator controlled by bus company MTL Trust, is to rehire 12 drivers made redundant earlier this month in an attempt to reduce the number of cancellations brought about by staff cuts. The drivers will work at the company's Leeds depot and will not be used to operate passenger trains. North East said it had cancelled 0.87 per cent of services since taking over the franchise on March 2. The cancellations followed the agreement of a productivity deal with drivers which led to 83 taking redundancy.
-- KIRCHGROUP CONFIRMS SEARCH FOR LARGE-SCALE BANK LOANS

KirchGroup, the German media group, confirmed Monday that it was in talks with banks over a large-scale loan believed to be in the region of DM1 billion (370 million stg). However, the group denied that the need for financing was linked to a cash crisis caused by increasing losses at its digital satellite television unit, DF1, and free-to-air networks SAT-1 and DSF. Kirch said that it had been in talks for some time with Bayerische Landesanstalt fur Aufbaufinanzierung (LfA), a publicly-owned bank which provides funding to small and medium-sized enterprises. The group is also thought to be in contact with a number of commercial banks including Bayerische Vereinsbank.
-- R&D PROGRESS REPORTS SPUR PPL AND SHIRE

Shares in biotechnology companies PPL Therapeutics and Shire Pharmaceuticals moved sharply on Monday after both groups reported progress in research and development. PPL shares rose 20p to 447.5p after the group said it had genetically engineered a rabbit to produce a human hormone called calcitonin in its milk. PPL estimates that the market for calcitonin, which strengthens bone structure, is worth $800m annually. Shares in Shire rose sharply before falling to close up 1.5p at 218.5p after the group said it expected "highly promising" results from its Lambda project, which is aimed at improving control of blood phosphate levels.
-- DATRONTECH FORGETS FALL IN MEMORY PRICES

Datrontech Group, the computer distributor, reported a 33 per cent increase in pre-tax profit to 8.1 million stg in spite of last year's fall in memory prices. Turnover rose by 59 per cent to 207 million stg on the back of a fourfold increase in memory volumes which offset falling prices. Chief executive Steve King said the group was committed to remaining the UK's leading memory distributor but would continue to diversify into higher-margin businesses such as communications and IT services. Memory last year accounted for 45 per cent of the group's business, down from nearly 60 per cent in 1995, Datrontech said.
